question: Research by Dr Attard, in Malta, involving 170 teachers, support staff, parents and children, confirms what many families already suspect: children with learning disabilities are not getting the tailored support they need. Thus while 75 % of educators said they understood autism, only 25 % felt confident adapting their classroom materials for autistic pupils.

This confirms parents’ fears that their children’s abilities may go undeveloped simply because the system cannot adapt to their needs. The EU Charter of Fundamental Rights guarantees ‘the right to education for everyone’, which implies education adapted to children with special needs.

Likewise, the European Disability Strategy stresses inclusive education and the integration of children with disabilities into mainstream schools with proper individual support. Across Europe, parents have raised similar concerns through petitions to Parliament.

Ensuring equal educational opportunities for children with autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) requires more than goodwill – it requires policy action. Could the Commission therefore clarify: 1.
What steps have been taken to implement Parliament’s resolution of September 2023 on harmonising the rights of autistic persons1?

What measures are currently in place – and what new policies are being developed– to ensure that children with learning difficulties, particularly those with autism and ADHD, receive the individualised education guaranteed under EU law?
OJ C, C/2024/1181, 23.2.2024, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/C/2024/1181/oj.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.11.2025) In the follow-up of 17 January 20241 to the Parliament Resolution referred to by the Honourable Member2 , the Commission highlighted ongoing action in the numerous areas covered. Further progress achieved includes the adoption of the European Disability Card3 and full implementation of the Disability Employment Package4, including through EU funding5.

Under the current mandate of the Commission, autism is being given further prominence in relation to health6. The Biotech Act7 and the European Health Data Space will support earlier diagnosis through advanced biomarkers, digital tools and development of therapy plans.

The European Reference Network ITHACA (Intellectual disability, TeleHealth, Autism and Congenital Anomalies)8 continues to work on diagnosis of developmental anomalies and coordination of multidisciplinary care and treatment.

In full respect of Member States’ competences in the area of education9, the Commission promotes inclusive education through initiatives such as Pathways to School Success10, aiming to achieve better educational outcomes for all. Measures include support to learners with disabilities, including autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

This encompasses accessible environments and learning materials, use of diversified teaching approaches and training of teachers and professionals. Together with Member States, mutual learning is fostered through the European Education Area Working Groups11. EU Cohesion Policy Funds can support accessible infrastructure and teaching methods/technologies for diverse learners.
Erasmus+ supports cooperation among stakeholders for developing capacities and innovative teaching materials enhancing inclusion.
